sentences: A market-day wrestling match unfolds on a single small album leaf.
People sit in a ring, and at the centre two wrestlers are locked together.
First, look around the whole scene as if you had squeezed in among the spectators.
The painter is Kim Hong-do, known as Danwon, the leading painter of late Joseon Korea.
He joined the royal painting bureau as a young man and went on to work on portraits of King Jeongjo.
This leaf belongs to his twenty-five-leaf album of genre painting, now a designated Treasure.
At upper left, gentlemen in wide-brimmed hats sit holding fans.
In front of them lie two hats that have been taken off, and a pair of shoes.
Among them, one man hugs his knees and holds his breath.
The spectators at upper right lean forward, hands pressed to the ground.
Some grin, some gape, some crane forward; no two faces are alike.
The drama of the moment is easiest to read in the crowd, not the wrestlers.
Now look at the two wrestlers at the centre.
The man in front has hoisted his opponent, whose leg is lifted clear of the ground.
Every ounce of strength is in the arms gripping each other's sash.
The viewers at lower right recoil, leaning back in surprise.
One reading is that the lifted wrestler is about to fall right in front of them.
Beside them, pairs of shoes that someone has taken off lie neatly in a row.
Look over the spectators along the bottom too.
One of these figures is famous for a 'mistake': his left and right hands appear to be swapped.
Whether it was an error or a deliberate joke is still debated.
Amid all this, only the young taffy seller on the left turns away, uninterested.
With his tray hung from his neck, he seems more interested in business than wrestling.
His indifference beside all that heat makes us smile.
Kim Hong-do left the background boldly empty and arranged the people in a circle.
Your eye therefore drops straight to the two wrestlers at the centre.
Deciding what not to paint is what shapes this composition.
Look closely at the wrestlers' legs: only a few quick ink lines pass by.
A light wash of colour is all that is added, yet you feel weight and muscle.
With a handful of brushstrokes, Kim captures not just a scene but its noise and heat.
Finally, step back and travel around the ring, reading only the spectators' faces.
Who is going to win?
This picture tells you through the crowd before the wrestlers ever do.
That is the genius of Danwon's genre painting.
